item.title: How Technologies Are Changing Five Industries: A Report from the Moscow Startup Summit
item.description:
Sergey Lavrov visited Sber's Moscow Startup Summit. Not the Minister of Foreign Affairs. I am a former entrepreneur, co-investor in two projects, winner of the reality show "Startup Battle," participant in Sber's accelerator for students, postgraduates, and university staff, and a graduate of "School 21." Therefore, I was interested in looking at the summit from different angles and understanding how the startup and venture ecosystem is structured today. Spoiler: after two days, I wanted to return next year as a startup founder or investor. The Moscow Startup Summit took place on September 29-30 at SberCity, in the "School 21" campus. For two days, startup founders, investors, representatives of corporations, and government agencies gathered here—four categories of participants were indicated on the badges to make networking easier. The scale is impressive: over 4500 participants from different countries, 150 experts, more than 40 discussions in the business program, and 100 startups at the exhibition. I walked through the key activities and sessions, and in this article, I will tell you what I saw. Read the report

item.title: The Word as Medicine: Zdravcity Turns Empathy into a Business Metric
item.description:
In an era of pervasive automation, genuine human interaction, free from robotic scripts, is becoming a business advantage and a customer retention tool. Service leaders agree that quality service is no longer just for handling complaints but a profit generator. At the V All-Russian Forum "Contact Center 2026" in Moscow, experts discussed the transformation of customer service. The key market insight is that while robots should handle routine tasks, only humans can retain customers in critical moments. Sincere attention during a problem is more effective than any promo code. The communication standard is also changing, with a complete ban on шаблонные phrases becoming a business imperative. When operators communicate live, using scripts only as a flexible framework, brand trust grows. The health marketplace Zdravcity.ru exemplifies this strategy's viability. Yuri Onosovsky, Head of Customer Service, shared the results of implementing an empathetic approach in the platform's unified contact center. The company uses three support lines for load distribution. Automation handles basic queries, while complex issues are escalated to the second line for individual handling, with professional pharmacists available if needed. Consequently, 82% of customers reach an operator within 20 seconds, and 95% of problems are resolved during the first call. Read more

item.title: Nano Banana 2.1 vs Nano Banana 2: three identical prompts and what the pictures show
item.description:
Google released Nano Banana 2.1 and promises improvements "across the board": quality, text in the frame, character consistency with multiple edits, infographics. I ran three identical prompts through Nano Banana 2 and 2.1 and evaluated the results using a checklist. The new version won in unexpected areas. I'll clarify the scale right away: this is not a benchmark. Three tasks, one run per model, one evaluator. Such a run shows where to look for differences, not measure them. I provide Google's numbers separately, and note separately: there are no independent measurements as of October 8, 2026, all publications about the release refer to the developer's single table. Read more

item.title: Decision Makers: A Russian Benchmark for Jev-style Models
item.description:
For the past couple of years, we've been using large language models in a rather peculiar way. Due to their versatility, we try to solve everything with them – request routing, moderation, evaluation, and much more. However, this setup is not very elegant from an engineering perspective: we have models that can hold conversations, code well, and write articles, but they spend a significant portion of their inference time answering relatively simple questions with two or three answer choices. This works, but it's like delivering a breakfast of syrniki using a huge truck, while the alternative is to train a separate model for each task. In September 2026, a distinct class of models emerged around this problem – Decision Models. On September 15th, TypeSafe introduced Jev, and since then, decision-making models have been appearing from all directions. I really like this class of models, which led to a simple question: how well does it work in real life, and can it be deployed to production? To answer this question, I constructed a benchmark to compare the quality, speed, and cost of decision-making. We will test both cloud and self-hosted models: Perplexity Decider 27B, TypeSafe Jev, Fastino GLiDE and GLiNER2.5-Decide, Cloudflare Clef 27B, OpenAI GPT-6 Luna Decisions, Liquid d1, Kev-9B, Cloudflare Clef-flash 9B, FRIDA-Decisions (and FRIDA Embedder), and Laya Typed Decisions. Let's go!

item.title: I Wrote a Vulnerability Scanner for AI-Generated Code and Tested It on 3,800 Repositories
item.description:
Today, a Telegram bot for selling VPNs can be set up in an evening: use Cursor, a few prompts, and it's already accepting money. But the bot token is in config.py, Postgres is exposed externally, and .env was left in the git history, 'deleted later.' I wrote a SAST scanner for AI-generated code and ran it on 3,800 public repositories. I'll explain what I found, how 16,378 raw findings turned into about 30 real leaks, and why I didn't check any of the keys I found. Read on.

item.title: How the Use of Neural Networks Has Changed the Gaming Industry and the Homebrew Scene
item.description:
The gaming industry has had a very complex development path: from something very local to mainstream for all ages, managing to almost die in 1983 and be revived by one company. And this path has always been accompanied by the evolution of development tools. Nowadays, the question of ethics in the use of AI for game creation is raised very often, and scandals sometimes erupt on this basis. In recent months, some truly incredible things have been created with the help of vibe coding and a little manual labor. Today we will talk about how AI accelerates game development, what it portends for the industry, and also look not only at how people create dream projects using verbal descriptions, but also how modern LLMs seem to have turned the homebrew scene upside down. Read more

item.title: MWS AI Vision Bench: What Has Changed in a Year and Why We're Adding Anti-fraud
item.description:
A year ago, we released MWS AI Vision Bench, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models on Russian-language documents. Since then, multimodal models have advanced significantly, VQA metrics have started to hit a ceiling, and we've added a crucial missing task to the benchmark: Anti-fraud. In this article, I'll detail how the benchmark has evolved and why tackling anti-fraud proved more complex than we initially anticipated.

item.title: FRIDA Decisions: Thinking Fast in Russian
item.description:
FRIDA Decisions is an open-source fast-thinking model for the Russian language. It selects an option from a list, assigns a score on a scale, answers 'yes' or 'no', and ranks candidates in a single encoder pass, without text generation, in tens of milliseconds on an RTX 5060 Ti. It can be used wherever LLMs currently function as classifiers or judges: ticket routing, moderation, data labeling, RAG ranking. On our razvilka benchmark, the model scores 0.893, on par with the commercial TypeSafe Jev API (0.897) and the LLM Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, which is 40 times larger. Read more

item.title: [Translation] Where did the AI agent break? How to debug multi-step workflows step by step
item.description:
A multi-step AI agent can give a convincing answer, even though the error occurred at the very beginning of the investigation. It's not easy to find it by the final result. We explain how step-by-step checks helped us localize failures and discover a bug in the evaluation mechanism itself. Let's break down the approach.
